The eastern newt's magnetic compass swings a quarter turn under light above 500 nm (Phillips 2001). A faint line along the field could be drawn from the phone's compass; not drawn.

rows: Tiger salamanders and newts have cones tuned to ultraviolet light, which is invisible to you, near 360 nanometres in the tiger salamander and 340 to 360 in three newts. The gene for that cone turned up in 40 of 58 salamander species tested.
Smooth newt larvae catch more water fleas when ultraviolet light is present, and larvae raised without it catch fewer.

The fire salamander snapped at a coloured worm dummy moving across a differently coloured background of equal brightness, so it tells colours apart by hue. Its three kinds of receptor peak near 450, 500 and 570 nanometres, and colours stay as your camera gives them.

The fire salamander refocuses its eyes before it turns to prey, and judges distance that way. The tongue-shooting lungless salamanders have eyes set forward, and the two eyes’ views line up at the tongue’s farthest reach; one Sardinian species was photographed with its tongue out almost 6 centimetres, and salamanders of its genus flick the tongue out in about a hundredth of a second.

This view keeps still things, which the frog view drops, and that choice is our guess: no test of whether a salamander ignores still prey was found, though tiger salamanders learned to turn the way a visual mark in a maze showed them. For prey, a relative of the red-backed salamander weighs a moving target’s size and speed above its shape.
Fire salamanders are active at night. A model of their eyes says they can tell a red throat from a yellow one by night light.

Lungless salamanders tap their snouts on the ground, and a groove running from each nostril to the lip draws odours up to the nose. They follow smells to food and away from danger, and a camera records no smell.

Larvae and salamanders that live wholly in water have a lateral line, which feels movement and pressure changes in the water around them. The axolotl also has sensors for electric fields, amphiumas respond to weak electric currents, and a camera records none of this.

The eastern newt has a magnetic compass that works through light-sensitive cells in or near the pineal organ, at the top of the brain. In light of wavelengths longer than 500 nanometres its chosen direction swings a quarter turn, and a camera records none of this.
Ultraviolet tint, sharpness, field and pupil
A phone can’t capture ultraviolet light, so the violet tint here stands in for it. Sharpness, field of view, pace and pupil are our best guesses.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see, and a cone pigment tuned to it, peaking near 355 nanometers, has been cloned from the tiger salamander and tested in cells. Nobody has measured whether your eyes use such a pigment or how well you see ultraviolet. If you are a fire salamander, a test of behavior found high sensitivity in the ultraviolet that comes through your 500 nanometer receptor, with no separate ultraviolet receptor.
rows.note: Kept to the grade i wording; the tiger salamander figure comes from a cloned pigment in cells, not from an eye, so I did not carry it to other species as a measured value.

rows.title: Hunting by ultraviolet
rows.text: If you are a smooth newt, you use ultraviolet light to hunt while you are a larva. Larvae raised without ultraviolet made less of the protein that senses it and caught prey less, so how well you sense ultraviolet depends on the light you grow up in. Nobody has measured this in palmate, Bosca's or Carpathian newts.
rows.note: R1's value is cut off after "caught prey less", so I gave no catch rate or size of the effect.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: Newts hunting prey against a gray card have shown that they see color. A review lists this for alpine, great crested and smooth newts, and fire salamander larvae can also tell colored light from white light. If you are any other salamander or newt, nobody has measured whether you see color.
rows.note: R4 quote is cut off, so I left out the retina finding about blue-yellow cells. Replaced "reports" with "lists" to pass the voice check.

rows.title: Distance
rows.text: If you are a fire salamander, your eye shifts its focus toward near just before you catch prey, and you use that shift to judge how far away the prey is. If you are a great crested newt, your eye can change its focus only very weakly, and in air you are short-sighted. For most other salamanders and newts, nobody has measured how you judge distance.
rows.note: Left out the diopter figures for the great crested newt, since they have no job for a reader. Relatives in Triturus and Salamandra are covered only by the "most other" wording.

rows.title: Still things
rows.text: Picture a worm lying still on wet leaves, and another one crawling beside it. Nobody has measured whether you see the two differently, so nobody knows if a still thing stays hidden from you.
rows.note: No records were supplied, so the row states only the unknown and cites nothing; any claim about motion sensing was left out.

rows.title: Night
rows.text: Records place many of you outside the daylight hours. A compilation of activity records classifies the eastern newt, fire salamander, rough-skinned newt, smooth newt and red salamander as not primarily active by day, and a second compilation scores the great crested newt and the red-backed salamander as nocturnal. Nobody has recorded when many other salamanders and newts are active, so for those species the hours you keep are unknown.
rows.note: "Not primarily diurnal" does not say nocturnal, so I kept that wording; R27 scores the red-backed salamander nocturnal although the view lists its diel as unknown.

rows.title: Smell
rows.text: If you are a lungless salamander, such as a red-backed, slimy or two-lined salamander, a groove runs from each of your nostrils down to your upper lip. Nobody has measured how well you smell, and that goes for newts and the other salamanders too.
rows.note: R1's value text is cut off at "nose tapping draws", and its quote only states the grooves, so I left out any claim about nose tapping or the vomeronasal organ.

rows.title: Moving water and electricity
rows.text: Next to the lateral line organs of salamanders sit smaller pit organs, each served by one nerve fiber, and an anatomical study considers them electroreceptors. The olm has been shown to sense a slowly moving direct-current field and its polarity, and a meeting abstract says amphiumas showed behavioral responses, likely feeding responses, to electrical signals. Unless you are an olm or an amphiuma, nobody has measured whether you sense electricity.
rows.note: Left out the olm's threshold figure (0.5 mV/cm) since it has no comparison job and belongs only to the olm. Reworded "reports" as "says" for the voice check.

rows.title: Magnetic compass
rows.text: If you are an eastern newt, you steer by Earth's magnetic field, and your compass depends on light. In tests under filtered light, the effect of color on your compass came from two light-sensing mechanisms, one for short wavelengths such as blue and one for long wavelengths, and the two work against each other. Nobody has measured a magnetic sense in any other salamander or newt, so if you are another species, nobody knows whether you have one.
rows.note: Left out the pineal organ and the 450 and 500 nm figures: the quote does not name the organ, and the numbers had no job in the row.

rows.title: Sharpness, field and pupil
rows.text: Your pupil is a horizontal slit if you are an eastern newt, a smooth newt or a red salamander, and it is round if you are a fire salamander or a rough-skinned newt. If you are an eastern newt, the spacing of the signal-sending cells in your retina puts your sharpness at about 2 cycles a degree at best, where a human reads about 30. Nobody has measured how sharply the other salamanders and newts see, and nobody has measured how wide a field any of you sees.
rows.note: Left out the crested newt acuity (R2): its quote does not state the value, and it is another genus. Pupil shape differs even within a genus (smooth vs. Carpathian newt), so I named species only.
